## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sattigumbajātaka* (Ja 503) is a story of the Buddha's previous births set in the Maddakucchi deer-park [Fausböll 1887]. According to the frame story, the narrative was prompted by Devadatta hurling a rock that splintered and wounded the Buddha’s foot; after the physician Jīvaka treated the injury, the monks remarked that Devadatta was a sinner keeping company with the sinful, leading the Buddha to explain that Devadatta had done so in past lives as well [Fausböll 1887].

The past story illustrates the power of environment and association through two brother parrots brought up in contrasting surroundings [Anandajoti 2010]. One parrot, Sattigumba, is reared in a robbers' village alongside a companion named Patikolamba, while the other parrot, Pupphaka, is nurtured in a hermitage of wise ascetics [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1887]. When a wandering king strays into their vicinities, Sattigumba urges the robbers to murder and plunder the king, whereas Pupphaka offers courteous hospitality, demonstrating how moral character develops according to upbringing [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1887]. In the birth identification (*samodhāna*), Sattigumba is revealed to be Devadatta, the robbers are Devadatta’s followers, the king is Ānanda, the ascetics are the Buddha’s disciples, and the Bodhisatta is the parrot Pupphaka [Fausböll 1887].

 Verses in the text correspond closely to the *Sukhapatthanā Sutta* of the *Itivuttaka* (Iti 76 / It 3.27, matching segment §23.1–27.6) and to the *Mahānāradakassapajātaka* (Ja 545, matching §21.4–27.6 with identical similarity) [DharmaNexus]. Further text sharing is noted with the *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka* (Ja 540) and *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547), alongside curated parallels with the *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532) and the Chinese *Jie jing* (T 765.124) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages automatically with the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
